articles.title: Apple Watch's AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Now in beta: Apple's new Audio Intelligence features can help you remember what someone said or take notes on conversations.
articles.body:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.

The news was announced via a press release sent out via Apple in India, but the update has not yet rolled out in the U.S. market as of this morning.

The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.

However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.

Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.

With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.

Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.

When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.

These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.

The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.

Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.

Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.

This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.

At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.

This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too.

Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.

Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.

The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.

The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.

To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards).

The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.

Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.

Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

articles.title: Apple’s India story is getting bigger: Record iPhone upgrades, Mac sales and services revenue
articles.summary: The iPhone still brings customers back to Apple in India and perhaps is the gateway to the hallowed ecosystem from Cupertino.
articles.body: The iPhone still brings customers back to Apple in India and perhaps is the gateway to the hallowed ecosystem from Cupertino. The September quarter offered a glimpse of what else they might buy once they’re there. Apple posted its highest-ever quarterly revenue in the country, with Macs and services also setting all-time India records. At the same time, CEO John Ternus said more people in India upgraded their iPhones than in any previous September quarter.Put those numbers together and there’s a more interesting story than another strong quarter for the iPhone. Apple has three ways to grow in India: sell an existing customer their next iPhone, persuade them to consider a Mac when they need a laptop, and earn from services in the years between those purchases. The earnings call showed strength in all three. It didn’t tell us how often the same customer was doing all three.The Mac record is particularly interesting because it works in both directions. An iPhone owner shopping for a laptop may give the MacBook Neo a look because it costs less than other MacBooks and works with a phone they already own. For someone replacing a Windows laptop who has never owned an Apple device, the Neo could be their first purchase from the company. Either would widen Apple’s reach in India in a way that selling a new Mac to someone replacing an old one wouldn’t.CFO Kevan Parekh credited the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro for global Mac revenue growth of 24% to $10.8 billion. Apple didn’t say which models drove the India record or how many buyers were new to the Mac. That is the detail to watch: a strong quarter for the Pro and a quarter in which the Neo wins over first-time Mac buyers can both produce record revenue, but only one tells you that Apple is reaching people who might never have considered a Mac.Services add another dimension. Someone can keep the same iPhone for years and still pay Apple every month for iCloud storage or spend money on the App Store. Globally, services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10% and more than a quarter of Apple’s $114.5 billion in quarterly revenue. Apple hasn’t said how close India is to that mix, or whether its local record came from more paying customers, higher spending by existing users or other sources of revenue.For years, a good quarter for Apple in India was easiest to read through the iPhone. That’s still where much of the attention will go. But the Mac and services records give us two more things to watch: whether Apple is becoming a serious option when Indians shop for a laptop, and what customers are willing to pay for after they’ve bought the device.You use AI every day. articles.body:
The competition is heating up on Dancing With the Stars , with just seven celebrities left in the race for the Season 35 mirror ball trophy.

The latest elimination came during Disney Night, when the couples performed routines inspired by musicals. Guest judge Wicked star Cynthia Erivo joined regular judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli.

The episode also featured a round of group performances, with the celebrities split into two teams joined by cohosts Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough.

Here's what happened last night and who was sent home.

Who left 'Dancing With the Stars' last night?

Julia Stiles and her professional dance partner, Ezra Sosa, were eliminated from Dancing With the Stars on Monday, becoming the ninth couple to leave the show.

The 10 Things I Hate About You actor performed a paso doble to "Satisfied" from Hamilton , earning 33 out of 40 points from the judges.

Stiles said her time on the show had been "an incredible experience," adding, "I pulled things out of myself that I didn't realize were there."

Sosa told Stiles it had been "an absolute honor" to watch her "growth in and outside the ballroom." He added, "I'm so lucky that I got to share this experience with you. I love you so much."

Meanwhile, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Dewan emerged as the night's highest-scoring celebrities, with both earning perfect marks from the judges.

Shum Jr., known for his role on Glee , joined partner Jenna Johnson for a jazz performance to "Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious" from Mary Poppins . The routine featured a live performance by Kyra Belle Johnson and earned the pair their second consecutive perfect score.

Dewan and partner Val Chmerkovskiy also landed full marks with a quickstep to "Be Our Guest" from Beauty and the Beast , accompanied by a live performance from Rodney Ingram.

Both celebrities joined forces for the team dances, performing alongside Connor Wood, Ezra Frech and cohost Julianne Hough as Team Wildcats. Their routine to "We're All in This Together" from High School Musical earned a perfect score of 40 out of 40.

The group beat Team Slaytopia, featuring Tatyana Ali, Maura Higgins, Amber Glenn, Julia Stiles and cohost Alfonso Ribeiro, which scored 36 out of 40 for its performance to "Zoo" from Zootopia 2 .

However, only one couple could receive immunity from the following week's dance-off. Shum Jr. and Johnson secured immunity after winning the tiebreaker, with a cumulative season score of 236 points compared with Dewan and Chmerkovskiy's 235.

articles.summary: Dane revealed he went to rehab 5 times while starring on the ABC show.
articles.body:
Eric Dane's posthumous memoir includes his experience on Grey's Anatomy.

The actor, who joined the show as Dr. Mark Sloan during season 2, went through a lot of personal ups and downs at the time.

Eric Dane 's posthumous memoir is a collection of life lessons for his daughters, including what he learned while playing Dr. Mark Sloan on Grey's Anatomy .

"Every moment I spend playing Dr. Mark Sloan, acting with the Grey's cast and interacting with the actors and crew off camera, is a complete joy," Dane wrote in My Book of Days: A Memoir in Moments , out now. While filming his first episode, "Yesterday," which aired in Feb. 2006, Dane felt "more fulfilled" than ever as he slipped into Dr. Sloan's scrubs.

Dane starred as the plastic surgeon, nicknamed "McSteamy," until his character's death in season 9. The actor returned to the show in 2021 for a special guest appearance during the show's 17th season.

Dane's final episode of Grey's came nearly three years before his amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis. The actor went public with his diagnosis in April 2025, less than a year before he died at age 53 on Feb. 19. (He's survived by daughters Billie, 16, and Georgia, 14.)

After shooting "Yesterday" as a guest star, Dane totally forgot about his work on Grey's. That is, until he got a call from a friend stating that he "hijacked the f---ing show." The reaction to his character was something "no one" had ever seen before (in the days before social media, no less), so Dane got a series regular offer.

Scroll through to read Dane's biggest Grey's takeaways from his posthumous memoir:

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

Dane wrote that he had "rocked" an audition for Dr. Derek Shepherd, the role that ultimately went to Patrick Dempsey. So when the opportunity to play Dr. Mark Sloan came across his desk, the actor was quick to turn it down.

"I could play the s--- out of this part. But I'm not going to. I pass," he wrote, concerned that Dr. Sloan would only be there for one episode. "Even though I tested for the lead, and almost got the part, I now have to audition for a guest shot? Call it ego, call it pride, call it stupid. I won't stoop to that."

Dane's wife at the time, Rebecca Gayheart . convinced him to take the audition. He recalled Grey's creator Shonda Rhimes being in the room. "Her presence makes me relax. I feel comfortable, as if I belong here," Dane wrote. The Burlesque star said he felt "a vibe throughout the room" as he read for the part.

"When I finish, I know, I just know. I nailed it. Shonda smiles," he continued. "The rest of the people in the room hold a beat, then they follow her smile, everyone now smiling and nodding, falling just short of gushing, and after our round of goodbyes, I leave, feeling high, feeling sure. I got the part."

After Dane officially joined the Grey's Anatomy , he realized it was a "dream job." The actor praised all of his costars — including Dempsey and Ellen Pompeo — calling them "princes and princesses" in the book.

"I fit right in, quickly assuming a lead role in our off-camera shenanigans. We're playing doctors saving lives, serious stuff. But once the director calls 'Cut,' I try to keep it light," he wrote. "We are not literally brain surgeons. We're actors, theater nerds. Our mission, if we choose to accept it, and I do, is to crack each other up."

Dr. Sloan makes his introduction to Grey's shirtless and wrapped in a towel — a pattern for Dane as he wrote "the scripts always call for me to go topless." Initially, Dane saw himself as "unremarkable, bordering on scrawny" when he got the gig. So, he got himself "in the best shape of my life."

Things changed, however, amid his tenure on the show. Dane hurt his neck working out and was prescribed painkillers. "My body goes to s---. I drop to 170, my face caves in, my eyes cloud, Iook gaunt; s---, I look like a drug addict. You can tell. I can tell," he wrote. "My attitude on set changes. I'm no longer bubbly, the fun guy, a ringleader in laughs. I don't act out. I don't throw tantrums or chairs. I go the other way. I bring everything inside. I dissolve."

Rhimes offered to help, and Dane turned her down.

Dane felt like he was "suffering" and didn't talk to anyone about it. "I can't help it. I feel other members of the cast looking at me. They're my friends. My work family. No. My family ," he wrote. "They don't judge me. They don't look angry. They look concerned. They look sad."

"I tell her I'm dealing with it. I lie to her. I lie to myself. I suck it up. Fight through it," the actor shared. "I don't want to be Shonda's burden. I don't want to be a problem. But I am. I am a problem."

During the course of Grey's Anatomy , Dane went to rehab five times. The actor wrote that he "improved" over time. His addiction was "managed," but noted that "things have changed" on set — and he "had enough" of being Dr. Sloan.

"Mentally, I'm on my way out," Dane wrote. "I love Mark Sloan, but I need to quit him."

Dane wrote that his addiction struggles were not what got him written of Grey's. It "comes down to money," he explained. "Despite Mark Sloan's popularity, I have become too expensive. I have become expendable."

The Last Ship star was "stone cold sober" when he ended his time on Grey's . "I go out strong," he added. "I make sure of that."

My Book of Days: A Memoir in Moments is out now.

If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health challenges, emotional distress, substance use problems, or just needs to talk, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7.

articles.title: Rivian spinoff Also wants to reinvent the wheel — but first, it has to ship
articles.summary: Also President Chris Yu opens up about surviving the AI server component crunch, rewriting UL battery standards, and why the company’s modular e-bike is just the first step.
articles.body: When Rivian quietly spun off its micromobility brand, Also, a lot of observers wondered if the luxury EV maker had bitten off more than it can chew. Chris Yu insists that’s not the case. Yu, a Stanford aeronautics PhD and former CTO at Specialized, runs the startup as an independent business that counts Rivian as a minority shareholder. Under his lead, Also rolled out the TM-B — a quirky, modular e-bike with a raft of unique features, including a swappable top frame, USB-C chargeable battery, a built-in screen, a series hybrid pedal-by-wire system, and proprietary “Dream Ride” software. There’s also the TM-Q, an electric four-wheeler aimed at commercial deliveries. But it hasn’t been completely smooth sailing. After dealing with supply chain headaches, confusing regulations, and some communication stumbles, Also is finally shipping its early Launch Edition bikes to customers while also getting ready to roll out the standard and performance versions. Meanwhile, customers have been letting the company have it on Reddit over the delayed deliveries, and the few people who have received their bikes have already experienced some minor software problems. The Verge met up with Yu to chat about scaling production, surviving parts shortages, dealing with the mess of US e-bike laws, and why the company is betting big on autonomous delivery. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. What is the current status of the bike and production ramp? On the bike, the main thing is the production ramp. It’s one thing to create a product as a traditional OE where you work with several Tier 1 suppliers, get them to deliver on time, and assemble it. With us, we’ve built and designed everything down to individual components and ICs. Over the last year, every imaginable supply chain learning has come across. We’ve been in the trenches competing with AI server demands for components like ICs, compute, memory, and raw PCBA [printed circuit board assembly] materials. Our inverter board is designed entirely in-house for high performance, and the thermals require a sophisticated board material. It turns out AI server farms have similar thermal requirements, triggering a global shortage, so we had to requalify and resource. But all that is behind us, and we are really starting to flow to customers and ramp up. A huge draw to come to Also was shipping a product that people will enjoy and use on the road every day, and reaching that milestone now has been huge for the team. How many bikes have you delivered so far? Are you still in the Founder’s Edition phase? That’s right. We’re quickly ramping up. We have a substantial number out there now, and you can see a lot of volume and traffic online of people taking their first rides. Deliveries are quickly increasing along the classic manufacturing ramp where you start steadily and then add volume. In hindsight, was targeting a spring launch too optimistic? At the time, based on everything we knew, spring was very much on plan. But as with Rivian on the automotive side or us earlier this year, a lot of unknown unknowns happened. Certainly I didn’t foresee the intense urgency around AI server hardware, nor the fact that those supply chains are so shared with light electric vehicles. "“Certainly I didn’t foresee the intense urgency around AI server hardware.”" - Chris Yu, president of Also Was there direct overlap between Also’s supply chain and Rivian’s? I look at it as a three-way Venn diagram between us — vertically integrated small EVs — and Rivian — full-size automotive EVs — and broader AI hardware like robotics and servers. There is a healthy overlap right in the middle, alongside direct overlap between us and Rivian. Where we overlap with Rivian there is a clear benefit, but it wasn’t easy for Rivian either. [Rivian CEO] RJ [Scaringe] and I talk all the time. Half the time we’re discussing how to handle a specific part or supply chain constraint. You either fight for the part and lean on suppliers, find an alternative supplier with the identical component, or — as both we and Rivian have had to do — completely redesign and requalify the system around a replacement part. [Image: The TM-B e-bike includes a modular top frame with swappable seat posts. Can you get specific on what components had to be redesigned or requalified? It sounds relatively boring on paper, but it’s critical. One example was IC components like high-performance capacitors. Swapping them requires the work of going through full validation testing to make sure the alternative hits our durability and lifespan standards, because those components dictate the reliability of PCBAs. Another was raw PCBA board material. Only certain base materials meet our flammability, thermal cycle, and structural rigidity requirements. When supplies ran short, we had to qualify third and fourth alternatives. There is no parallelization of verification testing — components must spend weeks inside thermal chambers and on shock and vibration rigs to prove they can handle real-world conditions. In a letter to customers, [head of product] Saul Leiken mentioned there were regulatory hurdles around power output as well. What happened with UL certification? It wasn’t so much an impediment as proof of how nascent the regulatory space is relative to what we’re building. Our battery combines several uncommon attributes: exceptionally high power density, an automotive-style software-defined battery management system with two-way flow for regenerative braking, USB-C 3.1 charging at up to 240 watts, and a removable pack. Those things combined don’t exist in standard e-bike battery guidelines. Certification bodies like UL write standards assuming a typical e-bike pack without USB data connections or such high bidirectional power throughput. When we presented our architecture, we identified undefined areas in the certification rules. Rather than treating it as a gray area and self-certifying, we partnered directly with UL to develop a clarification standard tailored to this type of battery architecture. We went back and forth, completed unit testing on both sides, agreed on the protocol, and we are now fully UL certified. Do you anticipate any thermal runaway problems, given how battery fires have plagued the e-bike sector? With any lithium-ion battery, you can never say never — whether you’re Tesla, Rivian, or an e-bike maker. Even from top-tier cell manufacturers like LG, Samsung, or Panasonic, there is an inherent cell fallout rate. Across thousands of vehicles and millions of cells, math dictates a non-zero number. That part is inescapable basic physics. Where we are super confident is our pack architecture. We took an exceptionally robust and conservative approach from both a mechanical and software protection standpoint, incorporating passive and active propagation defenses learned from generations of automotive EV battery design. The cell architecture, array welding, and management systems all benefit directly from that engineering. When do you anticipate starting deliveries of the Standard and Performance trims? Super soon. We have started opening reservation conversions, and anticipation for the Performance trim has been huge. We are focused on fulfilling orders for the supporters who lined up first and waited the longest, and the Performance line will follow right around the corner. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Early reservation holders on Reddit voiced frustration about communication gaps during the delays. What did you learn from that? I forget sometimes how much of a blessing it is for customers to care that much. It’s easy to make a product where nobody cares and there are zero Reddit comments. The responsibility is on us to be transparent. Our team’s default mentality was heads-down execution: chase suppliers, run engineering, and pass tests. We didn’t come up for air to keep everyone posted. That was a mistake on our part — not providing regular, transparent updates for the cohort that backed us early. We’ve changed that over the last couple of months, establishing regular communication with our preorder holders about what’s happening in production and what’s coming next. Did the delays trigger many order cancellations? Very few. Most people backed the project sight unseen, and since then almost everyone has attended a test event to try it out, which led them to double down. The overwhelming sentiment has just been: “I want it. When is it coming?” Between pedal-by-wire, swappable frames, and custom software, did you overcomplicate the bike when an off-the-shelf design could have shipped much faster? I don’t look at it that way at all. If we were to revisit the design, I would do the exact same thing. The largest untapped opportunity isn’t cyclists who already tolerate the current bike experience. It’s the massive demographic of people intrigued by leaving the car behind who haven’t opted in yet. Their hesitations are consistent: fear of theft, avoiding maintenance every two months, wanting seamless navigation and audio, and needing to carry a child without having to buy three different bikes. Solving those pain points requires a baseline of technology. Just like in automotive EVs, once you use software to personalize the ride and eliminate friction, people opt in. The majority of people attending our test rides haven’t ridden a bicycle in 10 or 15 years. Our goal wasn’t to go overboard; it was determining the minimum amount of innovation needed to create an experience as frictionless as stepping into a Tesla Model Y or Rivian R2. With cities and states cracking down on overpowered bikes and mopeds, how does Also fit into the shifting regulatory landscape? We are well-positioned by design to navigate a patchwork regulatory system. Current backlash is driven by bad actors selling products labeled as e-bikes that are actually mini-motorcycles, or bikes where clipping a wire uncaps speeds to 45 mph without vehicle safety standards. The primary issue is a lack of regulatory resolution between genuine Class 1, 2, and 3 e-bikes and unregulated vehicles, leading to blunt blanket bans like we’ve seen in New Jersey. Our philosophy is that the opportunity within legitimate Class 1, 2, and 3 categories is massive, and we remain definitively within that framework. We engineered the bike with immediate low-end torque so accelerating to 20 or 28 mph is responsive and fun without needing dangerous motorcycle speeds. Furthermore, because the bike is software-defined, the identical hardware can be configured to local rules — whether that’s 20 mph, 28 mph, or European 25 km/h limits. We are also introducing over-the-air parental controls so families can set conservative speed limits for younger riders, which is the exact opposite of the cut-the-wire approach. Were you concerned about delicate electronics or firmware falling out of calibration during shipping? Physical package handling was an early challenge. FedEx did not handle the initial deliveries well, so we paused and switched carriers, which resolved the issue. On firmware and calibration, it is a solved problem. Nobody picks up an electric car wondering if the drive-by-wire calibration got jostled in transit. Mechanically, the bike has very few moving parts. The drivetrain is fully sealed and pedal-by-wire, so traditional failure points like exposed derailleurs and shifters simply don’t exist. The down-tube computer, display unit, and hand controls are robust, solid-state systems rather than fragile instruments. What is the out-of-the-box assembly process like for non-cyclists? Very minimal. I pushed the team to make it feel as turnkey as unboxing an Apple Watch. You release a few clips, slide off the outer carton, and find three core elements: the main frame, the top frame, and the cockpit. The cockpit handlebar contains all integrated controls and wiring with a blind internal connector. Assembly entails mounting the front wheel, powering on the bike from shipping mode, connecting the mobile app, snapping on the modular top frame, and securing the stem base plate with two bolts. Threading the pedals is the final step, which is guided by short 20-second video walkthroughs in the app alongside a provided shock pump to set suspension pressure based on rider weight. How will service and repairs work for riders who don’t live near an Also brand hub? Many issues can be resolved over the air. When physical service is required, our onboard diagnostics pinpoint the exact issue immediately through data logs rather than requiring guesswork at a shop. If hardware replacement is necessary, we can dispatch parts proactively. Our repair network combines our own facilities with authorized local bike shops. We currently have roughly 150 vetted partners, expanding beyond 200 soon. We provide these shops with complete technical documentation, dedicated software tools, and direct parts inventory. Because every component board is digitally serialized to the bike for anti-theft security, authorized partners use our proprietary software to link new parts directly to the frame. Micromobility saw several high-profile company collapses after the pandemic boom. How does Also protect itself from those pitfalls? We didn’t start Also solely to be an e-bike company. The bike is our flagship and our handshake with the world, but our broader mission is building purpose-built small vehicles. The vast majority of urban trips are short, low-payload journeys — moving a single passenger or delivering takeout. Designing an urban transportation network from scratch would never rely exclusively on multi-ton cars. The bike serves as the architectural foundation for a broader vehicle roadmap that is software-defined, vertically integrated, and autonomy-first. Following the bike launch, we are heavily focused on autonomous delivery. Earlier this year, DoorDash joined as a strategic partner to develop and deploy autonomous delivery platforms. A light vehicle platform that carries payload across town at 28 mph offers significant cost-per-mile efficiencies, and our autonomous platform shares direct architectural commonality with that system. [Image: Cyclists ride Also TM-B electric bikes near the company’s headquarters in Palo Alto, California, in October 2025. Will that DoorDash collaboration result in a low-speed sidewalk robot? Sidewalk robots represent a completely different product class — closer to an industrial automated robot than an L4 autonomous road vehicle. By nature, sidewalk robots travel at 1 to 2 mph. While that works within localized, high-density environments like university campuses, purpose-built light electric vehicles operate at vehicle speeds across entire metro areas. I’m sure you’re aware there is some excitement going on around low-speed vehicles like golf carts. One hundred percent. And it does feel like this kind of fits into that. There’s been a ton of interest there. And that’s one of the more common questions I get is like when can we get one of these. But I think what you just said is actually – that’s the point that I want to focus on, which is – It’s less about the specific form factor of like a TM-Q or otherwise. It’s more the notion that there’s this huge gap and a huge demand for people to say, hey, the average household has something like two point something vehicles. And nearly everyone agrees that you don’t need two Escalades. You need like one big capable vehicle. And we’ve seen that a lot of people have started picking up things like golf carts and LSVs. And I would argue that it’s in spite of the deficiencies in the category. Because if you just think big picture, the problem that we’re trying to solve collectively is how do I have something that costs much, much less than an average-priced $50,000 car today? But at the same time, why does that have to be a crappy experience? I want that to be a premium experience and potentially be able to be L4 autonomous as well. And so for us, that’s a huge opportunity. So let’s take the notion of small purpose-built for getting around and doing the everyday trips that everyone does, but have it feel like a magical experience that potentially could be fully autonomous as well. That is a super interesting opportunity.

articles.title: Redmagic upgrades its liquid-cooled gaming phone with extra RGBs
articles.summary: The Redmagic 12 Pro adds RGB lights to its liquid-cooling system, though the results are middling.
articles.body: After introducing true liquid cooling to its gaming phones last year, Redmagic is upping the ante in its 12 Pro by building RGB lights into the transparent cooling loop, too. And they work! Sort of. The lights do turn on, and they can be set to glow in set patterns, activate for specific apps, or trigger for notifications and calls. The problem is that like last year’s 11 Pro, the cooling system itself uses fluorescent blue liquid, which the lights have to work against. Blue or white lighting just makes it look more blue, green turns out turquoise, and red or orange lights mostly produce colored bubbles swimming in a blue tide. The liquid-cooling RGBs are joined by a few other lights across the phone, with a small ring below the main camera, a side light that shines out from inside the chassis, and thin strips on the touch-sensitive shoulder buttons. Those don’t have the liquid to work against, so they shine in the intended color and often look quite different from the cooling ring. To complete the inconsistency, there are two strips of visible liquid cooling without RGB lights in the phone’s top-right corner, around and below the Redmagic logo, so those will be blue no matter what. Good luck getting all of this to match. [Image: [Image: [Image: The liquid cooling itself is improved beyond the lights, with output pressure of 130kPa, 85 percent up on the previous generation. It’s once again joined by both a built-in fan and a vapor chamber, which between them should be enough to keep the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 in check. It’s joined by 12GB or 16GB of RAM (the 24GB variant is seemingly a victim of RAMageddon) and 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of storage. The 8,400mAh battery should last a day or two, even while powering those lights and cooling, and the 80W charging is fairly fast. There’s an IP69 rating for water and dust resistance across most of the phone, though that may not count for much since the section around the fan is only IPX8, with no rated dust protection, making for a pretty large weak point. Existing Redmagic users may also be disappointed that the 3.5mm headphone jack has disappeared. The cameras are predictably basic, too: a pair of 50-megapixel rear cameras, one main and one ultrawide, neither with especially large sensors. The best thing about them is their design: completely flush with the phone’s body, sitting underneath the same glass panel that stretches across the rest of the rear. [Image: [Image: [Image: The other standout spec is the 185Hz refresh rate display, though like most high refresh rate displays, it hits the max speed only during certain compatible games. Redmagic boasts that this is the first 185Hz display to feature an under-display selfie camera too, one of those achievements that’s a record by virtue of its sheer specificity. The 16-megapixel camera here is very difficult to see — it’s much less visible than the iPhone Duo’s under-display camera — but photo quality is limited. It’s good enough for video calls, but selfies look rubbish, and it uses aggressive AI beautification features that as best as I can tell are impossible to turn off, perhaps to help mask how poor the quality is otherwise. [Image: My skin is not normally this smooth, and this is after turning off every beauty filter I could find. Redmagic isn’t immune to industrywide pricing pressure, so the 12 Pro starts at $949 — a $200 increase on the 11 Pro, and $100 up on May’s 11S Pro — climbing to $1,199 for the top spec. Every version includes both liquid cooling and RGB lights at least, which wasn’t true the last time around. Preorders start November 12th, with shipping from the 18th. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: The iPhone, MacBook and iPad price hike question Apple COO Sabih Khan ‘skipped’, and what Apple said about another increase
articles.summary: Apple is expecting memory costs to continue rising in the coming months, raising uncertainty about whether the company could increase the prices of its
articles.body: Apple is expecting memory costs to continue rising in the coming months, raising uncertainty about whether the company could increase the prices of its iPhones, MacBooks and iPads again. During Apple's earnings call on October 2, Apple COO Sabih Khan avoided giving a direct answer when an analyst asked about another price hike. However, CEO John Ternus and CFO Kevan Parekh shared details about how the company plans to manage rising memory costs. Apple CEO John Ternus said Apple is facing an “unprecedented” increase in memory prices. The company saw higher memory costs in the September quarter and expects the situation to get worse in the December quarter. Apple also expects memory prices to continue rising beyond December.What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," said Ternus. He said Apple saw higher memory costs in the September quarter, and the December quarter will be worse. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," he said.What did Apple COO Sabih Khan say about another price hikeDuring the earnings call, an analyst asked whether Apple could increase the prices of its products again to deal with rising memory costs. Khan, who took the question, did not provide a direct answer.Apple CFO Kevan Parekh said the company had made its recent price increases “reluctantly” and was trying to balance their impact. “I think what we try to do is evaluate, and in doing that, we evaluate the unit's revenue margin, and we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations. And we really believe we're balancing this well”.Apple expects a declining benefit from pre-purchasing memory over timeApple managed to offset some of the higher memory costs in the September quarter by using memory purchased earlier at lower prices. It also secured lower prices for some non-memory components. The company expects these measures to help cover part of the increase in memory costs during the December quarter. Apple also pointed to price increases across iPhones, iPads and Macs in June and September as factors that could help manage the pressure.However, Ternus said the benefit of buying memory in advance is expected to decline over time.Apple's inventory more than doubled year over year to $14.5 billion. Ternus also said the company's manufacturing purchase obligations increased by $33 billion between the June and September quarters.The iPhone-maker expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9% in the September quarter to between 45% and 46% in the December quarter. The company said higher memory costs and some Siri AI-related costs are expected to contribute to the decline.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.summary: Apple’s newest tablet has an improved OLED screen, a smaller and lighter design, and some new ruggedness. But $699 is a steep price to pay for an iPad Mini.
articles.body: The iPad Mini sometimes feels like a trap. It is, in some ways and for some people, the perfect iPad: meaningfully larger than my phone’s screen but still small and light enough to use for reading in bed or gaming on the subway. As most of the rest of the iPad line has tilted ever closer to laptop territory, the Mini might be the most iPad-y iPad left. I’ve taken a Mini everywhere with me since the very first one. But Apple only updates the Mini sporadically, and those updates sometimes feel like someone inside Apple Park picked its specs by closing their eyes and clicking randomly in an Excel sheet. The Mini is always a little underpowered, a little overpriced, and a little afield in Apple’s tablet lineup. We, the iPad Mini People, sometimes feel a little forgotten. This year’s model, though, is an upgrade through and through. Apple made the screen larger and better, while making the iPad itself smaller and lighter. It upgraded the processor in a big way. It made the whole package more durable, so you can take it to more places and use it for more things. It actually feels like a tablet made for a reason, not just another occasional bone thrown to the small-tablet fans. For the past week, I’ve been testing the midnight iPad Mini with cell service, 512GB of storage, and the nano-texture matte display coating. I really like it. It’s the best iPad Mini yet, and a huge leap over the previous model. The one in my hands also costs $1,249, and I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy it. Even the very cheapest version — Wi-Fi only, 128GB of storage, regular OLED display — starts at $699, by a wide margin the highest starting price ever for a Mini. If you don’t already know the iPad Mini is your one true love, there’s probably a better iPad out there for you. But if you’re an iPad Mini Person and you can stomach the price? You’re getting the best Mini in years. [Product: iPad Mini (2026) | The Mini’s new display is its most important and most controversial upgrade. It now measures 8.5 inches instead of 8.3, and it’s now a 2316 x 1512 OLED panel instead of an LCD. The OLED gives the screen a little more dynamic range than the previous model, with brighter bright spots and darker dark spots. Its peak brightness is noticeably brighter than before, and its minimum brightness is low enough to be totally pleasant for reading in the dark (as long as you’re in dark mode). In general, it’s just a little more crisp and contrast-y, in a nice way; the old Mini’s display was the least of my worries, but the OLED is a solid improvement. The tablet I tested also has Apple’s nano-texture matte finish, which seems to dull and darken the screen slightly; on a particularly white background, the whole thing seems to shimmer. I suspect I’d like the OLED panel even more without it. The nano-texture does, however, do an excellent job of reducing glare. The effect is actually really cool: The textured coating doesn’t extend to the bezels, so you can see a source of light or glare come in from the edge of the screen and then simply disappear as it hits the screen. So what you lose in pure screen fidelity, you gain in the ability to read on the iPad in a coffee shop without it reflecting the overhead lights like a mirror. The nano-texture option costs an extra $100, though, and requires you to upgrade to 256GB of storage, so you’re now looking at a $900 tablet. Spend the extra money on the cellular version or, better yet, don’t spend it at all. For some reason, Apple has never deigned to put its ProMotion display tech on the iPad Mini, which has a refresh rate capped at 60Hz rather than the 120Hz you’ll get on most other recent Apple devices. This is such an odd spec choice that it has launched a bunch of conspiracy theories. Maybe it’s to make more people buy an iPhone Duo instead? Maybe it’s a 120Hz panel downgraded to 60Hz by software just to make people upgrade again next time? Apple’s answer, to Chris Lawley and others, has been something to the effect of “120Hz is irrelevant, OLED’s faster pixel response solves the problems.” I don’t agree. I don’t think the lack of ProMotion is an immediate and total dealbreaker, but refresh rates matter! To games and high-touch creative apps, of course, but you notice the difference even with basic swiping and zooming. The Apple Pencil feels more juddery moving across my screen. On a 120Hz screen, I can scroll a browser page and still clearly read the text as it’s moving. With 60Hz, it gets blurry. In all these cases, even if you don’t explicitly see the difference, you really do feel it. [Image: I’m not saying you should read on an iPad next to fountain. I’m just saying you can. The most meaningful upgrade in the new Mini, at least for me and how I use my iPad, is that it is designed to be more or less waterproof and dustproof. Its IP67 rating means that the Mini got the highest possible score for protection from “solid foreign objects,” which for our purposes mostly just means dust won’t get inside, and is also “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water.” It’s not quite as rugged as, say, the iPhone 18 Pro, and I don’t recommend using it as an underwater camera or anything, but your tablet should be fine as long as you don’t drop it in the tub and leave it for a while. This increased ruggedness immediately changed my iPad usage in a couple of ways. I became less worried about handing the Mini to my toddler, whose general stickiness and penchant for spilling things no longer feel like threats. I also started using the Mini more in the kitchen — I love to cook with an iPad nearby for recipes and Community episodes, and it was nice not to be constantly guarding against flour explosions and water spills. At one point, the iPad Mini even came with me in the shower during a particularly close football game. It’s still kicking. The Mini’s IP rating is also the feature that finally made me see who Apple sees as the ideal iPad Mini user. This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad. We hear all the time about pilots who use Minis instead of sheaves of paperwork, but Apple also sees them in use on construction sites, oil rigs, doctor’s offices, and all kinds of other places. (It’s a fun rabbit hole, actually — can I interest you in an “explosion proof” last-gen Mini for $4,500 or so?) Apple’s goal with the Mini is not really to maximize performance, satisfy the pixel-peepers, or enhance creator workflows. It’s durability and usability. Body and screen. Apple made a couple of changes to the Mini to receive its IP rating, like ditching the speaker holes and opting for what it calls an Acoustic Display. It means the sound fires out of the front panel rather than from speaker holes. (Some TVs currently work the same way.) It doesn’t sound any better than before, maybe a tiny bit bassier, but it also doesn’t sound worse, and if anything it’s slightly better to have the sound actually pointed at you instead of out the sides of the tablet. Mostly it’s a wash in service of the ruggedization, which is good enough for me. The rest of the hardware is just wins all the way around. The A20 Pro chip, the chipset also on the iPhone 18 Pro (and the Duo), benchmarks about 50 percent faster than the 2024 Mini for standard computing tasks, and about three times as fast for graphics-intensive ones. (The chip in my review unit has one more CPU core than the A20 Pro in the cheaper Minis; those will still be drastic improvements, but maybe a hair less so.) I notice the difference, even side by side with the old model, in how fast apps load and games play. Games like Assassin’s Creed Mirage, which were all but unplayable on the 2024 Mini, work nicely on this one. The body is about a tenth of an inch thinner and about an ounce and a half lighter. Perhaps as a result, the battery is a tiny bit smaller, but battery life remains steadfastly somewhere around nine hours of screen time. [Image: Old model: speaker holes. New model: no speaker holes! One last hardware thing I should mention: Apple moved the front-facing camera from the portrait side of the Mini to the landscape side. On every other iPad, all of which seem to want to be used horizontally, that’s clearly the right decision. On this one, the only iPad I actually hold vertically for long periods, I’m torn. And in either case, that camera still doesn’t enable FaceID — it’s still TouchID or nothing on the Mini. I thought the last iPad Mini was a disappointment, a product made from spare parts without any particular reason for existence. This year’s Mini feels mostly like a return to form. It’s powerful enough to be useful for a long time. It’s lighter and thinner than ever. The 60Hz refresh rate is a bummer, but I don’t think it’s a dealbreaker for most people. And it’s really the only downside. Though at this price, should you have to deal with any downsides? After a run of new models and price increases from Apple, it’s worth level-setting a bit on iPad prices. The cheapest model you can buy is now the base iPad at $449, with an A16 chip (the one from the iPhone 14 Pro) and 128GB of storage. The cheapest iPad Air, with an M4 processor and 128GB of storage, is $749. The Pro has an M5 and 256GB for $1,199. iPads are expensive! In this context, the new Mini’s $699 starting price feels at least $100 too high — this model has always been more expensive than the base iPad, but unless you really want or need the small screen, $50 more gets you a much better and more versatile iPad Air. As ever, the iPad Mini is really only for iPad Mini People (and pilots and oil riggers, apparently). Someday, Apple will give us the tiny flagship we’ve been waiting for, and I’ll gladly pay Apple’s top dollar for it. This is a very good iPad Mini, but it’s not quite the Mini in its final form.

articles.title: Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
articles.summary: The Bambu H3C is a tool-changing, color-mixing, nine-nozzle printer that keeps your filament dry too.
articles.body: Three years ago, I told you how home 3D printers had evolved for speed, producing parts in minutes that used to take hours or days. Now, the next evolution is here: printers that can swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce nearly the full rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, and even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print. Today, Bambu Lab is announcing its most advanced 3D printer yet, the $2,499 H3C, which can do all of that mixing goodness — by loading nine different rolls of filament into nine different print heads. [Image: Nine rolls. Even if you’d never buy a printer this pricy, even if you’ve sworn off Bambu printers for good, the H3C is the perfect vehicle for me to explain where the state of the art in home printing tech is headed. While the H3C still only prints in one material at any given moment, Bambu’s new “Swaptek” system lets the printer swap in any of the eight other nozzles in six seconds flat. All nine tools are stored in a rack at the front of the printer, where they can independently preheat to the correct temperature right before they’re needed. [Image: Bambu’s “Swaptek” toolchanger system. With Bambu’s new “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, and white filament, I printed a beautiful rainbow bird feather that emulated most of the other colors between those inks. With a mix of flexible TPU and rigid PLA filaments, I was able to print a hard wristwatch housing with an integrated flexible watchband. With an ultra-soft “75A” TPU filament plus a harder 90A variety, I printed a breathable, wearable shoe that… didn’t quite fit, unfortunately. (I’ll measure and try again.) [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: To be clear, Bambu didn’t invent toolchanger printers or color mixing. You could even argue Bambu’s slightly behind the curve, particularly after the $700-$900 Snapmaker U1 and its four-color, five-second swaps pleasantly surprised the community earlier this year. (Prusa also sells its hotly anticipated 8-tool INDX system for $2,249, though I’ve heard it has some issues.) But I would have never bought previous toolchangers for myself, because they don’t have a place to keep your filament dry when you’re not printing. (Wet filament is one of the biggest remaining causes of print failures.) The H3C theoretically changes that by storing its nine rolls in an ostensibly airtight auto-loading container called the AMS 3H. Two of those nine slots even have built-in dryers that can hit 85 degrees Celsius and keep on drying your filament while you print, a big step up from Bambu’s previous AMS systems. [Image: Bambu’s wristwatch test print is an example of what’s possible with several different sizes of nozzle; I printed with the wrong nozzles so mine did not turn out this nice. I haven’t tried the H3C for long enough to tell you if it’s ready to buy, and I’ve definitely run into some quirks in my first couple weeks of testing. I’ve had to start every single print twice because the printer complains that its “toolhead camera” isn’t initializing properly, I once lost half a day of printing to a false-positive print failure detection, and the beta build of Bambu Studio provided to reviewers initially got confused when I tried to mix colors. (I’m told that last one will be fixed by launch, and Bambu eventually provided some troubleshooting steps for the toolhead camera close to embargo time.) You also have to load flexible TPU filaments into the H3C manually, and I learned the hard way that not all of the printer’s nine slots can actually accept a roll of TPU without causing trouble. Slot #6 can load standard filaments, but if you load the flexible stuff, another printhead can snag it and cause a nasty jam: [Image: Bambu’s fine print actually warns reviewers not to put TPU in slot #6 for multi-material prints, and this is apparently why. This also isn’t a printer where you can quickly repair a nozzle without tools, or use previous-gen toolless H, P, and A series swappable nozzles. It’s an all-new system that involves some minor disassembly, and I’m not sure about Bambu’s decision to leave filament in the toolheads between prints where it might attract moisture. [Image: But so far, this seems like an easier, more reliable printer than the two-nozzle Bambu H2D was at launch. Other than the Slot #6 TPU jam, which Bambu actually warns reviewers about in a section of the reviewer’s guide that I missed reading, everything I’ve tried to print has come out great so far — and without creating a mountain of little “printer poop” waste when I switch between colors! Dramatically reduced waste is one of the benefits of having extra nozzles. With any luck, the future of 3D printing won’t just be for hobbyists willing to figure out which colors of filament they need to order before each and every project, or obsessives who store dozens of colors in vacuum-sealed bags. Instead, it should be more like today’s inkjet printers — an entire rainbow of color, ready to go at a moment’s notice. And hopefully without all the inkjet printer shenanigans, of course. If you like Bambu’s toolchanger system, you probably won’t have to pay $2,499 for long. Certification filing leaks show that the company’s already prepping a smaller “P3C” with seven tools and seven rolls of filament storage instead of nine. [Image: The H3C is a very large, very tall printer with a large build volume. Compare it to my normal size P1P. Additionally, Bambu will let all three of its existing dual-nozzle printers print with two different sizes of nozzle by next spring, including the H2D, the H2C, and the X2D.

articles.title: Peak Design expands its collection of wireless charging accessories
articles.summary: Peak Design has a new collection of charging accessories, including a magnetic travel battery that supports the latest Qi standard.
articles.body: Peak Design, best known for its backpacks and travel bags packed full of useful features, announced it’s expanding its collection of chargers and charging accessories with new devices that focus on pairing premium materials with innovative functionality. “Somewhere along the way, we accepted that the electronics we use every day should be cheap, disposable and just good enough,” says Peter Dering, Peak Design’s CEO and founder. “We didn’t set out to make another collection of chargers and cables. We set out to show just how much better these everyday products could be.” [Image: The Wireless Kickstand Travel Battery supports the Qi2.3 standard so its 5,000mAh battery can wirelessly charge devices at 25W when connected to a USB power source. The $99.95 Peak Design Wireless Kickstand Travel Battery, available in a black or moon (cream) finish, wraps a 5,000mAh battery in a magnetic housing made from machined anodized aluminum with a matching folding kickstand. The company describes it as the “world’s first Qi2.3-certified wireless charger,” which is the latest iteration of the Qi2 spec. Most 5,000mAh battery cells can’t safely wirelessly charge a device at 25W. It’s a feature that’s more common with batteries with at least a 10,000mAh capacity. But by supporting Qi2.3, Peak Design’s new travel battery can wirelessly charge a compatible device at 25W while it’s connected to a USB power source. On battery power alone, its wireless charging speed maxes out at 15W. [Image: The Wireless Charging Station 2-in-1 has two 25W wireless charging pads that can be used simultaneously. Peak Design’s $99.95 Wireless Charging Station 2-in-1, available in the same color options as its new travel battery, is a Qi2.2-compatible accessory featuring a pair of 25W wireless charging pads that can be used simultaneously at full power. One of the pads is on the charger’s base that’s made from die-cast aluminum and zinc, while the other is attached to an adjustable arm that folds flat so the charging station is easier to travel with. [Image: The Dual Slim Charger is just a half-inch thick but can charge two devices with a maximum output of 65W. Neither of the new wireless chargers comes with an adapter, but you can pair them with Peak Design’s new $64.95 Dual Slim Charger that uses GaN technology so it’s just a half-inch thick but delivers up to 65W of power through a pair of USB-C ports. They’re joined by an assortment of new Peak Design USB-C UltraStrand Cables ranging from $24.95 to $39.95. The cables are available in lengths ranging from 15 centimeters to 2 meters for a 60W / 480Mbps version, or 15 centimeters to a meter for the 240W / 40Gbps option. Most of the new chargers and accessories are available starting today, but the Wireless Kickstand Travel Battery and certain lengths of the UltraStrand USB-C cables will be available a few days later on November 5th.

articles.title: Join us for the 2026-27 Tennessee basketball season on the SB Nation app
articles.summary: Our new game chats are perfect for the return of college hoops.
articles.body:
Almost two months ago, we announced the release of our new app, which you can find here or by searching SB Nation in your neighborhood app store. The app is available in North America, and we're working on Europe and the rest of the world as we speak!

Quite a few of you have downloaded it over the past seven weeks and have been using it, but if you are a big college basketball fan, it's also entirely possible a few of you missed it!

The goal with this app was to make it easier to join the community, and specifically comment, read the comments, and make your own posts, as well as keeping all the community posts – articles on the front page, Feed posts from you – front and center.

One of the most exciting new features is the game chat, which some of you may have already test-driven during the preseason. It makes it easier to follow along with the barrage of comments that come during games, and gets to the heart of why so many of you spend time in our community. Faster loading comments and notifications when someone replies to your comments and Feed posts are creating a more fun experience that you're not going to find anywhere else.

We also wanted to elevate the community's contributions by putting your Feed posts inside one stream alongside all the other articles from the site. To that end, more people have seen your posts and more people have commented on them. In fact, we've set single-day commenting records three different times in the last several weeks.

And if you prefer just reading our traditional front page articles, there's an option at the top to do that.

So, thanks for making us part of your routine. If you haven't checked it out, you can get the app for iOS or Android . And if you're not an app user, that's OK! We're glad to have you following along in whatever way makes you most comfortable.

College hoops fans, game day is better on the SB Nation app!

React to every crossover, alley-oop, and block alongside fellow basketball fans in real time.
